subtopic_detail: Pathway to gender affirming hormone treatment for a competent adolescent in Australia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in an adolescent clinic seeing a 15 year old who was recorded female at birth, attends with both parents, and asks you to start testosterone. He has consistently described himself as male since the age of nine, uses a male name at school, and says the distress about his chest and periods has worsened each year.

Both parents support him and say the request has been consistent for years. He is in year 10, attends school daily and has close friends. Breast development is complete and he has been menstruating for three years. He describes his reasoning clearly, understands that some effects of testosterone are permanent while others are not, and asks about fertility preservation without prompting. He denies self harm and has no current suicidal thoughts.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, height on the 60th centile, blood pressure within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, renal function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a multidisciplinary gender service for assessment of readiness and competence
options.rationale: Australian standards place hormone treatment inside a multidisciplinary assessment covering diagnosis, mental health, competence, fertility counselling and family support, and referral is what actually moves this young person towards treatment (Source: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.text: Apply to the Family Court for authorisation before any hormone treatment begins
options.rationale: Court authorisation is no longer required where the adolescent is competent and the parents and treating team agree, and insisting on it now adds cost and delay that Australian case law removed (Source: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.text: Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue to suppress further puberty
options.rationale: Puberty suppression is the intervention for an adolescent in early or mid puberty, and at completed breast development with three years of menses there is no remaining pubertal progression for it to prevent (Source: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.text: Commence testosterone today with a written treatment agreement and monitoring
options.rationale: Prescribing before the multidisciplinary assessment skips the fertility, mental health and competence components that Australian standards place before initiation, and initiation sits with the specialist service (Source: RANZCP: Recognising and addressing the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria).
source_refs: RANZCP: Recognising and addressing the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

options.text: Advise that no medical treatment can be considered until he turns eighteen
options.rationale: There is no age of eighteen threshold in Australian practice, and deferral of this kind is associated with worsening distress rather than with a neutral wait (Source: RANZCP: Recognising and addressing the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria).
source_refs: RANZCP: Recognising and addressing the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

explanation.summary: Care for trans and gender diverse young people in Australia is organised in stages, with puberty suppression available in early puberty, gender affirming hormones considered from mid adolescence, and surgery generally deferred to adulthood. Australian law changed in 2017 so that court authorisation is not required for gender affirming hormone treatment where the adolescent is competent to consent and the parents and treating team agree, and a court application is now reserved for genuine disputes about competence or about the treatment itself. Assessment is multidisciplinary because coexisting depression, anxiety, autism and eating disorders are common and change the sequencing of care without removing the indication. Fertility counselling occurs before hormones start, since testosterone reduces fertility and oocyte preservation is easier before treatment. Ongoing monitoring covers haematocrit, liver and lipid profiles, bone health and mental state.
key_points: Court authorisation is not required when the adolescent is competent and parents and clinicians agree.
Puberty suppression applies in early to mid puberty, not once pubertal development is complete.
Assessment is multidisciplinary and covers mental health, competence, family support and fertility.
Fertility counselling and preservation options are discussed before hormones are started.
Deferring all care to adulthood is not a neutral option and is associated with worsening distress.
explanation.pearls: Testosterone raises haematocrit within the first months, so a baseline and six monthly full blood count is standard and a haematocrit above about 0.50 prompts dose reduction rather than cessation.

sources.label: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents
RANZCP: Recognising and addressing the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

subtopic_detail: Conducting a first mental health assessment when the accompanying relative is interpreting
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 42 year old man who arrived in Australia two years ago and holds a bridging visa. He has come about eight months of daily headaches and broken sleep, and his 16 year old son has come to translate for him.

Through his son he says only that his head hurts and that he is tired. When you ask about his mood, he looks at the floor and the son answers that his father is fine and just needs tablets. Physical examination including neurological examination is normal and there are no red flag features for the headache. He shakes his head when the son asks whether anything happened before he came to Australia, but you notice his hands begin to tremble.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no papilloedema, no neck stiffness, blood pressure within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the consultation with his son translating and explore his mood directly
options.rationale: A family member as interpreter, and a child in particular, filters what is asked and answered, exposes the young person to distressing material, and is a recognised barrier to disclosure of trauma (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

options.text: Engage an accredited interpreter by telephone and continue the assessment today
options.rationale: An accredited interpreter, available free to practitioners through the national service, allows the son to leave the room and lets you explain confidentiality and its independence from visa status before asking about trauma (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

options.text: Refer directly to a specialist torture and trauma service without further assessment
options.rationale: Specialist referral is likely to follow, but sending him on without a basic assessment or an explanation he can understand risks non attendance and leaves the headache unexplained (Source: Australasian Society for Traumatic Stress Studies: Working with refugees and asylum seekers).
source_refs: Australasian Society for Traumatic Stress Studies: Working with refugees and asylum seekers

options.text: Prescribe mirtazapine for the insomnia and review him again in four weeks
options.rationale: Prescribing without a diagnosis treats a symptom that is likely to be one feature of a trauma related disorder, and it confirms his son's framing that tablets are what is required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Ask him to return with a written translation of his symptoms at the next visit
options.rationale: Written translation places the burden on the patient, may not be possible if he has limited literacy in his own language, and defers an assessment that can be completed now (Source: Australasian Society for Traumatic Stress Studies: Working with refugees and asylum seekers).
source_refs: Australasian Society for Traumatic Stress Studies: Working with refugees and asylum seekers

explanation.summary: People from refugee backgrounds carry high rates of post traumatic stress disorder, depression and somatic presentations, and headache, back pain and fatigue are frequently the presenting complaint rather than psychological symptoms. Disclosure depends on conditions the clinician controls: a professional interpreter of the right language and dialect, ideally not from a small local community where confidentiality feels uncertain, and an explicit statement that the consultation is confidential and separate from any immigration process. Using a relative, and especially a child, distorts the history and imposes a burden that has its own harms. Insecure visa status is itself a potent and ongoing stressor that worsens outcomes independently of past trauma. Trauma focused therapy is effective in this population, but stabilisation of housing, income and immigration uncertainty often has to run alongside it.
key_points: Use an accredited interpreter rather than a family member, and never a child.
State explicitly that the consultation is confidential and separate from immigration processes.
Somatic complaints such as headache and fatigue are common presenting symptoms of trauma related disorders.
Insecure visa status is an ongoing stressor that independently worsens mental health outcomes.
Specialist torture and trauma services accept direct referrals but a basic assessment should precede them.
explanation.pearls: The national Translating and Interpreting Service is free for medical practitioners consulting people who hold a Medicare card, so an accredited interpreter can usually be on the telephone within minutes rather than being deferred to a later appointment.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health
Australasian Society for Traumatic Stress Studies: Working with refugees and asylum seekers

subtopic_detail: Acting on fabricated illness in a child when only one observer reports the events
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see the mother of a 3 year old girl on the paediatric ward. This is her seventh admission in fourteen months for reported episodes in which she stops breathing and goes blue.

Every episode has been witnessed by her mother alone, including two that were reported as occurring in the bathroom during previous admissions. Prolonged video electroencephalography over four days recorded no events and no epileptiform activity, and cardiac, metabolic and airway investigations have all been normal. Nursing staff document that the girl is playful and eats well, and that she has had no episodes across three nights when her mother was not on the ward. Her mother trained as an enrolled nurse, has researched the condition extensively, and has requested transfer to a fourth hospital.

data_table.Examination: Child alert, playful, growth on the 50th centile for weight and height, no bruising and no injuries
data_table.Investigations: Four day video electroencephalography with no recorded events, echocardiogram normal, metabolic screen normal, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Discharge home with a monitor and outpatient paediatric review in two weeks
options.rationale: Sending the child home returns her to the environment in which the reported events occur, and monitoring equipment tends to generate further reported alarms rather than to protect her (Source: RACP: Child at risk guidelines).
source_refs: RACP: Child at risk guidelines

options.text: Arrange covert video surveillance of the mother in the ward cubicle
options.rationale: Covert surveillance has a limited place, requires formal legal and institutional authorisation and police involvement, and cannot be arranged by a treating team acting on its own initiative (Source: RACP: Child at risk guidelines).
source_refs: RACP: Child at risk guidelines

options.text: Notify child protection services and convene a multidisciplinary case meeting
options.rationale: Repeated presentations reported by one observer, extensive negative investigation and absence of events when the reporter is away meet the threshold for a mandatory notification, and the statutory service rather than the ward team then leads the assessment (Source: RACP: Child at risk guidelines).
source_refs: RACP: Child at risk guidelines

options.text: Interview the mother alone and put the inconsistencies in the history to her
options.rationale: Confronting the reporting parent before protection is in place risks flight from the hospital, escalation of the fabricated illness or an abrupt change of hospital, which is why disclosure follows rather than precedes notification (Source: RANZCP: Factitious disorder imposed on another).
source_refs: RANZCP: Factitious disorder imposed on another

options.text: Repeat the neurological workup with extended ambulatory monitoring at home
options.rationale: Further testing is the mechanism by which harm accumulates in this presentation, since each investigation carries risk and validates the reported illness without adding information (Source: RANZCP: Factitious disorder imposed on another).
source_refs: RANZCP: Factitious disorder imposed on another

explanation.summary: Fabricated or induced illness in a child is a form of child abuse, and the psychiatric diagnosis sits with the perpetrating adult while the paediatric response is driven entirely by the child's safety. The warning pattern is a persistent illness that does not fit any recognised course, symptoms and signs witnessed only by one carer, resolution when that carer is absent, extensive negative investigation, multiple institutions consulted, and a carer with medical knowledge who is comfortable in hospital settings. Doctors sustain the harm through investigation and treatment, so recognising the pattern requires reviewing the whole record across hospitals rather than the current admission alone. Notification to the statutory child protection service is mandatory for medical practitioners in every Australian state and territory and does not require certainty, only reasonable suspicion. Siblings must be considered as well, since mortality in this form of abuse is substantial and other children in the household are frequently affected.
key_points: Events witnessed by only one carer that stop when that carer is absent is the central warning pattern.
Mandatory notification requires reasonable suspicion, not proof, and applies to all Australian medical practitioners.
Do not confront the carer before protective arrangements are in place.
Further investigation perpetuates the harm and rarely adds information.
Assess siblings, who are frequently affected and are at risk of the same harm.
explanation.pearls: Assemble a chronological record across every hospital the child has attended before the case meeting: the pattern is almost never visible within a single admission and becomes unmistakable when presentations, investigations and negative results are laid out on one timeline.

sources.label: RANZCP: Factitious disorder imposed on another
RCH Melbourne: Child abuse clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: First line treatment choice for established post traumatic stress disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 29 year old paramedic nine months after a highway crash in which the driver she was treating died. She reports vivid intrusive images of the scene several times a day, wakes at three most mornings after the same dream, and has driven a forty minute detour to avoid that stretch of road every shift since.

She startles when a colleague drops equipment and has stopped attending the station debrief because the talk brings it back. Her mood lifts at home with her partner and she has not lost interest in her hobbies. She drinks two standard drinks a week, uses no other substances, and has no delusions or hallucinations. She has taken no medication and asks what will actually help.

data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged, hypervigilant to noise in the corridor, no psychomotor retardation, no anhedonia
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What treatment would you recommend first?

options.text: A single session structured psychological debriefing about the crash
options.rationale: Single session debriefing does not prevent or treat the disorder and has been associated with worse outcomes in some trials, which is why it is no longer recommended in Australian practice (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

options.text: Trauma focused psychological therapy delivered over eight to twelve sessions
options.rationale: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing are the recommended first line treatments, with larger effect sizes and more durable benefit than medication in adults who can access them (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

options.text: Sertraline titrated to an effective dose with review at four weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor is the recommended pharmacological option and moves to first line when therapy is unavailable, declined or ineffective, but it sits behind trauma focused therapy when that is accessible (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Diazepam at night for the sleep disturbance and morning waking
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not treat the disorder, impair the extinction learning on which exposure based therapy depends, and carry dependence risk in a young person facing months of treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Non directive supportive counselling with her workplace employee service
options.rationale: Supportive counselling helps with practical stressors but does not target the trauma memory or the avoidance, and it performs measurably worse than trauma focused therapy in head to head trials (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

explanation.summary: Post traumatic stress disorder is diagnosed when intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal persist beyond a month after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence. Australian guidelines put trauma focused psychological therapy ahead of medication for adults, and both cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing carry the same first line recommendation. Medication is added when therapy is unavailable, declined, or has not produced adequate benefit, and when a comorbid depressive disorder needs treating in its own right. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, with depression, alcohol use disorder and other anxiety disorders each present in a substantial minority, and identifying alcohol use matters because heavy drinking undermines exposure based work. Occupational groups repeatedly exposed to trauma, such as paramedics, police and firefighters, need the diagnosis considered explicitly rather than attributed to the job.
key_points: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation are equal first line treatments.
Medication is second line for adults unless therapy is unavailable, declined or has failed.
Single session debriefing is not recommended and may worsen outcomes.
Benzodiazepines impair the extinction learning that exposure based therapy depends on.
Screen for depression and alcohol use disorder, which are common and alter the treatment plan.
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the serotonin reuptake inhibitor most often started in Australia for this indication, and the trial should run eight to twelve weeks at an adequate dose before being called a failure, which is considerably longer than clinicians typically allow.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Impaired control over gaming with functional collapse in a final year school student
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 17 year old brought by his father after failing three year 12 subjects. For about eighteen months he has played an online game for eight to ten hours a day, mostly overnight, and has told his parents he was studying when he was playing.

He quit the soccer team he had played in since he was eight and no longer sees the friends he played with. He has twice tried to cut back to two hours a day and lasted a few days each time. When his father took the console away last month he shouted, punched a door and did not sleep. He describes himself as absorbed and content while playing and flat and restless when he cannot. He drinks no alcohol, uses no other substances, and his weight and appetite are unchanged.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect that brightens when discussing the game, no psychomotor retardation, no thought disorder, no self harm
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with withdrawal and loss of interest
options.rationale: Depressive anhedonia is pervasive and would not spare the activity itself, whereas he is absorbed and content while playing and his sleep loss is a consequence of the schedule rather than early waking (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Social anxiety disorder with avoidance of peers through online activity
options.rationale: Social avoidance here followed the gaming rather than preceding it, and he played team sport socially for years without fear of scrutiny (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).
source_refs: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria

options.text: Adjustment disorder in response to academic pressure in year 12
options.rationale: An adjustment disorder follows an identifiable stressor and would not explain a pattern that began eighteen months before the academic decline and that produced it (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).
source_refs: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria

options.text: Gaming disorder with impaired control and functional deterioration
options.rationale: Impaired control over gaming, escalating priority over other interests and daily activities, continuation despite clear harm, and a duration beyond twelve months with school, sport and friendship losses meets the diagnostic pattern (Source: World Health Organization: ICD-11 gaming disorder).
source_refs: World Health Organization: ICD-11 gaming disorder

options.text: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder presenting as academic failure
options.rationale: That diagnosis requires symptoms present before the age of twelve and across settings, and he sustained schoolwork and a team commitment for years before this pattern began (Source: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Gaming disorder is recognised in the international classification as a disorder due to addictive behaviours, and it is characterised by impaired control, increasing priority given to gaming over other interests and daily activities, and continuation or escalation despite negative consequences. The behaviour must normally be evident for at least twelve months and must cause significant impairment in personal, family, educational or occupational functioning, which is what separates it from heavy but harmless play. Most adolescents who game for long hours do not have the disorder, and the diagnosis rests on functional collapse rather than on hours alone. Comorbid depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder are common and need separate assessment, since treating an underlying disorder often reduces the gaming. Family based intervention and cognitive behavioural approaches that build alternative reinforcement are the mainstays, and abrupt confiscation without a replacement plan tends to produce the kind of escalation his father encountered.
key_points: Impaired control, escalating priority and continuation despite harm are the three core features.
Duration is normally at least twelve months with clear functional impairment.
Hours played alone do not make the diagnosis; loss of function does.
Screen for comorbid depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
Abrupt device removal without a replacement plan commonly escalates conflict.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about failed attempts to cut down and about what happens when access is removed: two or more self initiated failed attempts plus an angry dysregulated response to enforced abstinence discriminates the disorder from heavy recreational play far better than any hours threshold.

sources.label: World Health Organization: ICD-11 gaming disorder
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD
